claim_text: SBP Branchless Banking Regulations (revised 30 Dec 2019), Section 9.1(b): AFIs must publish their schedule of charges for BB activities quarterly at branches/agent locations/website, and charges cannot be increased during a quarter
source: SBP, Branchless Banking Regulations (Revised Dec 30 2019), Banking Policy & Regulations Department

claim_text: The 2019 SBP Branchless Banking Regulations, read in full, contain no explicit textual clause stating that cash-in transactions must be free of charge to the customer as a general rule (the only 'free of cost' language found relates to viewing the last 5 transactions, and to account-opening/closing charges and biometric-verification cost specifically for Home Remittance Accounts)
source: SBP, Branchless Banking Regulations (Revised Dec 30 2019) -- direct full-text read

claim_text: SBP Branchless Banking Regulations Section 3.2(a)(v) defines Cash-in and Cash-out as a permissible activity via bank-branch counters, ATM machines, and authorized agent locations, without specifying a fee/no-fee rule for either side of the transaction
source: SBP, Branchless Banking Regulations (Revised Dec 30 2019) -- direct full-text read

claim_text: CGAP's cross-market description of the 'typical' P2P wallet transfer model treats cash-in as free to the customer, with the agent earning a commission paid by the provider; cash-out costs the customer a fee, and the agent earns a commission on that too -- this is a general model description across CGAP's 4 study markets (incl. Pakistan), not a Pakistan-specific regulatory citation
source: CGAP, "Wallet and OTC Transactions: Understanding Financial Incentives" (Cook & Rashid, Aug 2017)

claim_text: CGAP Pakistan-specific commission/pricing benchmark on a US$20 transaction (fieldwork period ~2013-2016): customer pricing -- formal OTC 5.70%, wallet 'full loop' 1.85%; agent commission -- formal OTC 1.95%, cash-in/cash-out (wallet) 1.30%
source: CGAP, "Wallet and OTC Transactions: Understanding Financial Incentives" (Cook & Rashid, Aug 2017)

claim_text: CGAP notes that target-based compensation for sending OTC transactions is paid to some agents depending on the franchise, and that 'anecdotal evidence suggests such compensation can account for up to 60% of agent MFS revenue' -- CGAP itself labels this anecdotal, not measured
source: CGAP, "Wallet and OTC Transactions: Understanding Financial Incentives" (Cook & Rashid, Aug 2017)

claim_text: CGAP's 4-country comparative fieldwork (provider/agent interviews, agent mystery-shopping, and Central Bank data across Pakistan, Ghana, Tanzania, Bangladesh) classified Pakistan as a 'low informal OTC market,' and concluded that agents across the studied markets, including Pakistan, do not typically have or use significant commission-driven leverage to steer customers toward informal/off-book transactions ('Do agents have a proverbial thumb on the scale...? Not really.')
source: CGAP, "Wallet and OTC Transactions: Understanding Financial Incentives" (Cook & Rashid, Aug 2017)

claim_text: No independent Pakistani source (press investigation, SBP consumer-protection circular, or complaint record) was found in this research pass describing agents routing customer cash-out transactions through their own personal wallet or bank account -- as an ordinary P2P transfer -- specifically to avoid the operator's commission share and keep a self-set commission entirely
source: Research pass across SBP circulars, Profit/Business Recorder/Dawn/ProPakistani archives, and CGAP Pakistan-specific fieldwork; no direct source found

claim_text: No independent source was found confirming a widespread, documented practice of Pakistani BB agents charging customers for cash-in specifically (as distinct from cash-out, which is openly fee-bearing on published tariffs)
source: Research pass; only an unattributed, non-citable forum discussion thread referenced 'shopkeepers deducting Rs 10-20 extra,' discarded as unreliable

claim_text: Profit by Pakistan Today (2021) reported an industry source warning that, to recover revenue lost from the SBP's 2021 IBFT fee waiver, operators 'might resort to charging a fee for each cash-in at a branchless banking agent,' which the source called 'contradictory to digital financial inclusion' -- this is evidence of a live commercial pressure toward charging for cash-in at the company-policy level in 2021, not of an existing agent-level personal-account workaround
source: Profit by Pakistan Today, "Why the SBP has JazzCash and EasyPaisa on their toes" (Taimoor Hassan, 19 June 2021)

claim_text: Telenor Microfinance Bank (Easypaisa) fee/commission income was Rs6.3bn in 2020 (vs Rs5.9bn interest income) and Rs8.2bn in 2019 (vs Rs9.2bn interest income); the bank ran losses in both years
source: Profit by Pakistan Today, "Why the SBP has JazzCash and EasyPaisa on their toes" (2021), citing Telenor Microfinance Bank financial statements

claim_text: SBP's 2021 circular instructed banks/MFBs/EMIs to keep IBFT transfers up to Rs25,000/month free of cost to the individual customer; beyond that limit, institutions may charge up to 0.1% of the transaction, capped at Rs200
source: Profit by Pakistan Today (2021), describing the SBP circular (primary circular text not independently opened in this pass)

claim_text: Published 2026 cash-out (withdrawal) fee tiers: JazzCash charges Rs35 on Rs0-1,000 rising to Rs400 on Rs40,001-50,000; Easypaisa charges Rs7 on Rs1-200 rising to Rs690 on Rs40,001-50,000 (15-tier slab structure, common across licensed BB providers)
source: Pakistan Observer, "JazzCash vs EasyPaisa Cash Withdrawal Charges in Pakistan (2026 Update)" -- a secondary tariff-aggregator source, not the operators' own official Schedule of Charges document

claim_text: BISP beneficiaries withdrawing their payment through a digital wallet under the new interoperability system pay a PKR 280 cash-withdrawal fee; online transfers and Raast transactions remain free; SBP told a National Assembly Standing Committee it will revise the schedule of charges every six months

claim_text: An easypaisa Digital Bank executive, in a Business Recorder / BR Research interview, argued that cash needs to be made more expensive than digital payments in order to shift customer behaviour toward digital channels

claim_text: CGAP's analysis of Easypaisa's own OTC-to-wallet transition documents a structural incentive misalignment: the agent earns a recurring commission on every OTC transaction, but only a one-time fee when a customer activates a wallet -- meaning it is in the operator's interest to convert OTC customers to wallets, but not in the agent's interest
source: CGAP, "The EasyPaisa Journey from OTC to Wallets in Pakistan"

claim_text: No dataset or analyst report was found in this research pass isolating a measured decline in branchless-banking agent cash-in/cash-out transaction volume attributable specifically to Raast's growth; Raast's threat to the agent commission model is best supported as a structurally plausible, anticipated risk (per industry executive commentary and the operators' own historical fee-revenue dependence), not as an already-occurring, measured effect
source: Absence-of-evidence finding across SBP Payment Systems Quarterly Reviews, BB statistics series, and available fintech/analyst commentary
